utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are present. From the Defence teams I only notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic, Mr. Krgovic and Mr. Haynes. The Prosecution team today consists of Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. Mr. Bourgon, where is he? We have been told you have a preliminary, we know what was what it is all about; the motion hasn't been filed as officially as yet unless it has been filed in the last few minutes. We were suppose today have a courtesy copy at least our senior legal officer. Is the Prosecution au courant with the subject matter of your would be motion? Sorry to have cut it just to economize our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges. Good morning colleagues. The Prosecution also received a courtesy copy on Friday afternoon it was briefly discussed over the phone, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there an objection from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, so in expectation of the motion that will be received, we granted beforehand

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically that's it. Your motion is granted and you can -- you have these photos included in the 65 ter list, which of course you can make use of. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. President. I have two more preliminaries I would like to discuss with the Trial Chamber this morning. The first one has to do with the scheduling of Witness 3DW-1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me, 3DW?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 1, who is our expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I need to go into private session to raise this issue, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The second preliminary issue has to do also with Witness 3DW1. He is scheduled to testify beginning on Thursday morning of this week, and we have been in contact with him, and he has asked the Defence whether we at all possible to end his testimony by Friday the next day in order to complete the testimony in two days. With the present estimate that is we have, this is a tight fit. Although it is possible, we would be short about half an hour, maybe an hour to complete his testimony on Friday. Again, I've informed my colleague of this issue and the question this morning is would the Trial Chamber be prepared to go into an extended session on Friday afternoon, if this is possible of course from a logistics point of view, in order to end the testimony of that witness on Friday. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course I need to consult with my colleagues on this, of course everyone has commitments like you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position is as follows: Towards the end of the week we will be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis because Judge Kwon has got other duties to attend to, official duties. It so happens that on Friday afternoon, my colleague Judge Prost quite early in the afternoon has a commitment of her own, in other words, she can't be here for a prolonged sitting. The sitting will have to end at the scheduled time. However, we are thinking of suggesting to you if this is acceptable to not just to you and the Prosecution, but to all the others, if we on Thursday instead of starting at 9 o'clock in the morning we start at 8 o'clock in the morning. And that applies also to the staff, technicians and everything. I know that exceptionally it is done but for it to happen we need to have the the agreement of everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wake up early anyway at 6 a.m. I'm up usually, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank the Trial Chamber for this information. This is the reason why I raise it at this time. From our point of view, Mr. President, there will be no problem starting with 8, but I need to consult with everybody else before I can give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You do that and once you have sort of reached an agreement or et cetera, then you need to consult with your respective clients in other words each one of you please consult with your respective clients before you talk to Mr. Bourgon, particularly, because I don't want to create problems for anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is one final preliminary issue which I think has become a non-issue, but there were conversations between the Prosecution and us concerning the scheduling for the following week because on Tuesday the 30th is a holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is a holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There were discussions that maybe there could be no sitting on Monday to allow for a long weekend, Mr. President, in order to prepare; but we are not asking for this and the other -- my colleague from the Defence may very well ask or not ask from the Prosecution side I was informed this morning they are no longer look for this day or we are not looking for that day either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Depends whether or not it disrupts your plans to finish your case on the first week of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The consequences as I informed the Prosecution yesterday of course if we take that day then for sure we will not be able to finish by Friday the 3rd. If we work on that day it's a possibility that we will finish, although it is not a guarantee we might have to go a bit into the following week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Think further about it and let us know. We are here to work, in other words we will all be here on Monday available, but we'll await for further feedback from you in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Finally just to inform the Trial Chamber that there might be a short gap in the scheduling tomorrow. We have two witnesses lined up today, we are not sure whether we will be able to complete both witnesses today. If so, that would leave only one witness for tomorrow before we do the video conferences on Wednesday. So just so inform the Trial Chamber that there might be some free time at the end of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We are ready to proceed with our next witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Bring in the witness, please. Mr. Bourgon, when is your Thursday and Friday witness 3DW1 arriving here?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: He has arrived last night, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can't you start him off tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, because he has been away for some time and he has something that is already scheduled that he is attending also in The Hague, and we told him he was beginning on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words he can't spare one hour tomorrow and start off.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, I can certainly ask him and see if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thanks. Good morning to you, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are most welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth. The text is going to be given to you now, please read it out aloud; and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Kostic. Please make yourself comfortable, have a seat. Mr. Bourgon, whom you have already met, I suppose, is going to put a series of questions to you. He will then be followed by others on cross-examination. Mr. Bourgon, he is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For the record allow my to introduce myself, my name is Stephane Bourgon. And along with my colleague Ms. Jelena Nikolic and Ms. Marie-Claude Fornie. We represent Drago Nikolic in these proceedings. I have quite a few questions this morning and I would like to simply invite you that if there are any questions that you do not understand, do not hesitate to stop me so we can clarify those questions, do you understand this sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Stevo Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What is your date of birth and what is your age?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The 27th of May 1956. I'm 52 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: In a place called Vitinica near Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How close is this from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Around 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, before the war, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I completed high school. I worked in the auto transport company in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because it is specific, I'm going to ask the next question, did you play any sport before the war?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Which sport did you play, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I played soccer for the Drina soccer club.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, today what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I'm currently unemployed since my company went bankrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And just to come back to the last question, the Drina football club, I take it this is a professional team, is it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I played professionally for the Drina club while working on my regular job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, correct me if I'm wrong, but you were mobilised during the war in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you were a member of the Zvornik Brigade in 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you work for any company or battalion in particular?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Military Police Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the military police company?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The commander of the MP Company was the then-lieutenant Miomir Jasikovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the year 1995 what was your position with the Military Police Company?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: In 1995, I was the clerk of the MP Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you the clerk of the Military Police Company throughout the war or did you do something else before?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in the military police, I did the same tasks as other military policemen did -- as of February 1993, I became the clerk and I remained in that position until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as the clerk of the Military Police Company, can you describe your duties? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I kept the list of attendants in the MP Company. I made rosters for the company. And in the morning at lineup, I would read out daily orders, and all the other jobs that were necessary for the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, who maintained the personnel records of the Military Police Company?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: It was me who maintained it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you describe your normal day of work during the war, as a clerk of the Military Police Company?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: In the morning, when we got up there would be a lineup and the hoisting of the flag. If there were no combat activities to be expected, we would continue to read out the orders for the day, which I had prepared the evening before. Of course that had to be approved by Commander Jasikovac. I had to read that out in the morning and then the military police went about following the tasks that had been issued to them. The lineup would be followed by breakfast and then everyone had their own respective tasks in the barracks at Standard or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yourself, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I had an office that I shared with Commander Jasikovac and I spent most of my time there. I was usually in Standard or in the office, whatever the duties may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you a picture at this point in time. This picture is for in e-court please, 3D490. This picture will appear in front of you on the screen, and I would like you to take a look at this picture, and I will ask you a question. Sir, do you recognise this picture, and if so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the entrance of the command in our building. I can see here the window of the office where we were. That is to say, the room that belonged to the MP Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At this point in time, sir, I will ask the court usher to provide you with a pen, this is a special pen that allows you to write on the screen; and I would like you to indicate on this picture and to indicate the number 1 on the window of the office you occupied along with Lieutenant Jasikovac.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you put a circle around this 1.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, although this is an obvious question, can you put the number 2 at the main entrance of the command building?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And put a circle around the 2.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you can at the bottom of this -- of the screen, if you can indicate today's date, as well as your name and initials.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you can put 3DW15, so that we know that this is markings that you made. I can repeat those figures. 3DW15. Thank you. My next question is sitting from your office could you see visitors coming into the main building or to the main command building?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We won't be needing this picture anymore, although there are more coming. Sir, my next question is do you know who Cedo Jovic and Goran Bogdanovic are?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you tell us who they are and if you knew them in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I did know them, of course. They were members of the MP Company, but they were there as lawyers. They were in the department for combatting crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was there any other lawyers that you know of in the Military Police Company?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you share the names of these lawyers with us?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: In addition to Bogdanovic and Jovic, there was also Nebojsa Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know where was the office of the lawyers or of the legal department where Jovic, Bogdanovic and Jeremic worked?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will now show you another picture which is in e-court 3D496, and again I will ask you to do some markings on this picture. First take a look at the picture that will appear in front of you, and then I will ask you a question. Sir, do you recognise this picture.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: It's also the command building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you know where the window of the office occupied by the legal department was?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like you to use the pen that will be given to you by the court usher, and to indicate the number 1 on the window of the office occupied by the legal department.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you can put a circle around this 1.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And again at the bottom of this drawing, if you can put the date, your initials, and the same number 3DW15.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks] What else do I need to write, 3D?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The same number, 3DW15. My next question, sir, is from this window, is it possible to see the main entrance of the Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The lawyers you mentioned earlier, did they work in the same office or did they have more than one office?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: All three of them were in the same office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, we won't be needing that picture any more, but there's more coming up later. Sir, did you as the clerk of the Military Police Company go to the field along with the other military policemen?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: There were such instances when I was sent into the field. A few times when the lines came under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Was that something that happened regularly?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I did go two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as the clerk, after 1993 did you perform any duties like the other military policemen did?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And before you became the clerk, did you perform any duties in the Standard barracks, like the other military policemen?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I joined the military police in December 1992. My tasks were that -- were the regular military policemen tasks, I was at the gates, I was at the bridges, and took part in any apprehensions, if there were any. Regular -- the regular military police tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as a clerk after 1993 did you perform at any time these other tasks, for example, on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you perform any tasks, were you ever at the gate after 1993?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier the morning lineups. Where were these -- how did these morning lineups were conducted?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: There were lineups for the whole barracks just before breakfast. I don't remember any more at what time exactly. Each of the units would have their own lineup, our MP company would be headed by Commander Jasikovac, the rank and file soldiers were lined up. I would come forward and read out the daily orders. That's it. And the same goes for the rest of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did Jasikovac have a deputy to run the Military Police Company?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who was the deputy?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: His deputy was my younger brother Aco Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know Drago Nikolic and did you know him in 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you know what was his position in 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: He was head of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, did you have any dealings with Drago Nikolic for work purposes?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I did not. Drago Nikolic communicated with Jasikovac. I knew Drago Nikolic, we would greet each other, but we had no dealings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did Drago Nikolic work with the legal department?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: We was in contact with them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us when Drago Nikolic and Jasikovac communicated as you mentioned at line 6, what did they talk about?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I think that every morning the commander met his associate issuing them tasks for the day. After that the chief of security, Drago Nikolic, would see Jasikovac; Jasikovac would go to his office and he would issue orders to him if there was anything to be done by the military police. Therefore, they would meet and talk about the things we were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for a clarification for the record, there's a reference to the commander meeting his associates, I think we probably all know what or to whom that refers but if we could just clarify commander versus "komandir" or precisely who we are talking about there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was going to thank my colleague for his ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you mentioned that the commander met with his associates. Who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Commander Pandurevic would you have an early briefing with his immediate associates meaning the chief of security, the head of the brigade of logistics; and they would agree on the things that were supposed to be done that day. After that the chief of security, if there were any tasks of the military police, apart from our regular duties, he would see Jasikovac and issue him with certain tasks that we would see through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did Jasikovac attend a meeting with Commander Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Maybe occasionally, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you, yourself, did you attend that meeting with Commander Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when there were meetings between Jasikovac and Drago Nikolic, did you attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, sir, did Drago Nikolic issue orders to the members of the Military Police Company?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Drago did not issue orders to us, Jasikovac did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. What about the personnel records of the military police, what was Drago Nikolic's involvement with these records?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how many members were in the Military Police Company of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Around 90 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you tell us about the organisation of the Military Police Company, how was it organised?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The MP Company performed solely the police tasks. There were three platoons; there was formally speaking the apprehension platoon, the traffic platoon, the security platoon; they were supposed to provide guards at the gate, et cetera. And they were involved in the military police tasks. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to go back, my colleague is bringing my attention to something that you said. In terms of the dealings between Lieutenant Jasikovac and Drago Nikolic, at page 15 lines 14 to 16 you mentioned that Drago Nikolic would issue orders. And later on you spoke about taskings that were issued by Drago Nikolic -- to Jasikovac. Are we talking about orders or taskings?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, tasks. I think that when Jasikovac went to see him for these briefings that he was given tasks. He was told what we were supposed to be doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, that is just to clarify one issue. Were there any drivers in the Military Police Company?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember who suppose drivers were in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Stevic was the driver of Commander Pandurevic. Milorad Bircakovic was the driver of the chief of security Drago Nikolic. Those of us who were members of the MP Company had two drivers who drove our minivan, Drago Acimovic and Mirko Matic. We had another driver who would come only occasionally and was given work details, he also drove a minibus.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did Jasikovac have a driver?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What role did the military policemen play in terms of, or in respect of deserters?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The military policeman would bring in military deserters into the Standard. If a battalion notified the MP of certain soldiers having deserted their positions, then the military police would bring them in to the Standard in Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So was there a detention facility in Standard?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who was kept in this detention facility?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: This was the detention facility for our deserters who left their positions. So it was for our members or other members of our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did the battalions of the Zvornik Brigade have any military policemen?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How many, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. There may have been two in each. I believe that one battalion even had three of them, I can't really remember at this time. At any rate, every battalion had a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the military policemen who were with the battalions, were they included as part of the Military Police Company of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did these military policemen change or were they always the same one with each battalion or was there a rotation?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: They rotated. There was policemen who spent longer period of time in a given battalion because they were well acquainted with the situation on the ground, but other than that, they did rotate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did the military policemen of the company perform any kind of duty on the bridges between Zvornik and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what was that duty; can you describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The military police held the Karakaj bridge, the Sepak bridge, and the Zvornik bridge for a while. There was also the civilian police force and the customs staff there. The military policemen had to check all the military-aged men on their way to Serbia. All those who wanted to go to Serbia and who were of military age had to have a permit for that purpose. This was their task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how many military policemen were at the, take them one by one, the Karakaj bridge, for example?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Approximately one to two. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of those who were responsible for this bridge or who had this as a specific tasking?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: They rotated. There weren't the same policemen every day. I made a roster for them, one day they would be assigned to the Sepak bridge, another day to the Karakaj bridge, and then still other to the Zvornik bridge, and there were several policemen who were assigned to the bridges. They worked in two shifts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat the last sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, can you repeat the last sentence please because the interpreters didn't catch you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, that they worked in two shifts. There was the first and second stint and then overnight there were no military policemen at the bridge, there was only the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if we turn back to Standard, what other duties did the military policemen perform at Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Members of the Military Police Company were at the gate at reception box there and this was their non-stop duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did they perform any other duties in Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned that one of the duties performed by the members of the Military Police Company was to be at the gate. You said at the reception box there, and we will come back to that. Was there any other duties that they performed at Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The military policemen who were on duty at the gate took note of those entering the barracks compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my question was not precise enough. Other than the gate, were there any other duties performed by military policemen within Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were there any other duty that is you remember of?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were. Not all the policemen were at the gate. They rotated there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like now to show you a picture which is for e-court please, 3D497. We will use the same procedure, it will appear in front of you. I would ask if you take a look at it and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, could my client be excused for a few minutes, the trial can continue in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I just wants to make sure since there are always a limited number of guards, that this is possible. If you could wait one moment, Mr. Gvero. Do you think you can work this out? Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are grateful to the security staff. Apologies to my learned friend and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the picture that is in front of you, and if so, what is it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the reception area where the military policemen were located when they were on duty at the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, to the left of that picture, we see a building in the back. What building is this?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: This is the command of our brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you explain what was in that office where the military policemen on duty at the gate were? Can you describe that office, what was there?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Normally there were two policemen on duty at the gate. One was inside the reception office and would take note of those going into and out of the barracks. Whereas the other policemen would stay outside the office in order to lift the swing gate for the vehicles entering or leaving the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, if I look at the right of this picture, there's the gate there. Do you recall what that gate was for in 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. The soldiers or civilians entering the Standard barracks would pass through there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, for the record, Mr. President, the witness was referring to exhibits -- at least to picture 3D497 until it becomes an exhibit, and I would like to now have in e-court 3D500.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, a new picture will appear in front of you, and we'll use the same procedure. I would like you to take a look at the picture and tell you [sic] what it is?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I see the entranceway to the Standard barracks. The gate through which the vehicles would enter the barracks compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, with the assistance -- do you see on this picture the barrier that needs to be lifted to let cars in and out?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like you, to -- using the pen given to you by the usher, can you put a circle around the barrier that was lifted to let the cars in and out?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, when was this picture taken, if you know?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: A month or two ago, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you present when these pictures were taken?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, what you draw -- can you explain what is it that you draw a circle around?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: This is the gate, how should I put it? This is where the barrier was lifted for vehicles to pass through. The barrier itself was dismantled as there is no need for it there at present. Otherwise, it used to be there, and it had to be lifted for the vehicles to pass into or out of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, was there also a gate that could be rolled out in front of the entrance to Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you see this barrier on this picture, can you put a circle around it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you put the number 2 beside the circle?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the picture, same procedure, put the date, your initials, as well as number 3DW15, please.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Please. Thank you, we won't be needing that picture anymore. I'd like to have in e-court now 3D502.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are discussing, and it did occur to us before, but we let you go now perhaps it has gone a bit too far to remain simple, but when we are not dealing with protected witnesses, is there any special reason in your mind why you would use 3DW, or whatever? For example, I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To make it shorter for the witness instead of writing his name, writes a number. But for us the names and numbers are the same whether the witness is protected or not, the only thing that changes is adding the letter P when it is a protected witness, and Mr. Kostic is not a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, I think we need to continue while we started with this witness this way, we have to continue this way, but and for you is it problematic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, think about it, Mr. Bourgon, we think it would be more simple and straightforward if we just have the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My mistake, Mr. President, I will get the witness to write his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a question of a mistake, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kostic, can you just above that number, can you write in block letters your name?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I know we can't do it now because the picture has been frozen so we'll leave it like this and move on to the next. If I can have now 3D502 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the counsel information, to be enough the initials of the witness or the signature, there's no need for the witness number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, madam registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, there's a new picture before you. Do you recognise this picture and can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the entrance to Standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you put a circle around the office where the military police on duty at the gate was.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks] This is where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And put the number 1 in this circle.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you also put a circle around the place where the lifting barrier used to be.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And put a number 2 in this circle.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And also put a circle around the barrier that could be rolled out in front of the entrance of the Standard barracks. And put a 3 in this circle.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would now ask you that you put the date and simply your initials at the bottom of this picture.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, we won't be needing that picture anymore. Sir, what did the military policemen on duty at the gate do, what was their function there?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Their duty was to check who was leaving or entering the standard barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did they check all the vehicles coming in or out -- or going out?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Military vehicles leaving or entering the barracks were driven by individuals who they were well familiar with since they would see them there every day, and they didn't particularly check them. Civilian vehicles did not enter the barracks compound except for a commander or a military officer who happened to drive a civilian vehicle, but then of course they would not be checked. Other civilian vehicles were not entering the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, what was the procedure, if you remember, for checking a civilian vehicle coming in to Standard barracks? And I'm talking about a civilian vehicle with a civilian driver?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, if a civilian showed up at the reception area, he had to leave the vehicle by the entrance where there was a large parking-lot. He would then approach the gate and the police -- military policemen would ask for his ID and for -- and would ask him who he was going to see inside the barracks. The military policeman would then write down his personal details from the ID and would make a telephone call, depending on who the individual was about to see, to check if that particular individual could be let through, and if so, he would then allow him to pass into the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And once this procedure was over, and if the visitor was approved to go in, how did that take place?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The military policeman would escort him to the office where this particular individual was meant to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How many military policemen were usually at the gate?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Normally there were two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were they supposed to note the arrival time and departure time of any visitors coming in?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. They noted the ID number and the ID would be kept at the reception area until such time as that individual returned on his way out of the Standard barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that when it was a military vehicle driven by a known driver, that they would not be checked or controlled, or that they would be let in. To your knowledge, from the time, if a civilian vehicle came in, was it possible to miss a civilian coming in?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No. This particular gate was the only entrance into the Standard barracks. Whoever wanted to enter the barracks, had to go through the reception area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What was the procedure when the visitor who had been allowed to go to the -- to somewhere inside the barracks, when the visitor left, what was the procedure?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: When the visitor returned, the departure time would be noted, his ID returned and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, to your knowledge, would the military policeman on duty at the gate ever allow unknown visitors to walk freely into Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, if a visitor came in and wanted to see the commander of the brigade, would the military policeman at the gate know whether the commander was present or not in Standard?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: He probably would because the commander had a car. Besides, if the commander had to leave, then he would have left through the gate. Otherwise, the operations duty officer would be the one to be asked if anybody wanted to see the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned the car of the commander, was it parked in view of the military policeman at the gate?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If the commander had been away for some time, what would the military policeman at the gate have to do to confirm whether the commander is there or not?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: He would say that the commander was not there and would not grant access to the visitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe my question was not put properly. If the military policeman on duty at the gate for some reason did not know whether the commander was present or not in the barracks, what could he do in order to verify this information?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: He would call the duty operations officer and ask him whether the commander was there and whether he could see the visitor. I think that was the procedure at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, just to clarify, you say I think that is the procedure. Are you sure or do you know whether this was the procedure?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's what the procedure was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to focus your attention now to the year 1995, and more particularly July 1995, a few days after the fall of Srebrenica. Do you recall this period in general?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the Military Police Company was doing during this period?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The MP Company was in the field most of the time because the Srebrenica Muslims were going through the area of responsibility of our brigade. They were in the field. There were a few military policemen in the barracks at Standard performing their regular duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What do you recall, sir, if anything, concerning Muslim prisoners being driven by bus in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I saw them pass by on the buses. I saw Muslims on board those buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you describe what you saw, exactly; what you remember seeing?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I saw that there were civilians on those buses, men with their heads bent low. They passed by Standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were there many buses that passed in front of Standard to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Quite a few buses, but I wasn't looking out on the road all the time. I saw a few of the buses pass by.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what time was that, if you recall, sir, that the buses passed in front of the Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly. I think it was around noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, the -- if I use this day that you see the buses as a point of reference, do you remember f the members of the military police Company who were at Standard, whether they were sent anywhere the night before?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Where were they sent, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: They were sent to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who sent them there?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Commander Jasikovac. He arrived and said that the rest of the military policemen that were at Standard should get ready to go to Orahovac to secure the Muslim prisoners of war that were there. He said that they should all get ready to go and secure those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you yourself go to Orahovac that night?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I got ready to go because he said everyone should go. After that in the course of the day, the UNPROFOR arrived at the Karakaj bridge. I think it was just before it got dark. They could not go across and somebody had to stay behind to provide security for UNPROFOR. He told me to go to the bridge to provide security for those UNPROFOR members, therefore I didn't go to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, that night that the Military Police Company were given instructions and they left to go to Orahovac, and that they were given those instructions by Jasikovac, did you see Drago Nikolic at all in Standard barracks that night?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing Drago Nikolic earlier that day at all?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly. I may have seen him but it was quite sometime ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember who was the military policemen on duty at the gate that night?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: At the gate it was Jeremic, Nebojsa during that night. I think before him it was Milomir Simic I'm not 100 per cent sure of that, but I think he preceded Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when, just to clarify, when the military policemen left for Orahovac, did Jasikovac go with them?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During the night that you spent at the Karakaj bridge, did anything special happen that night?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I was at the bridge the whole night until the next morning. I don't know what was happening elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what happened the next morning, sir, to you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The next morning I returned to Standard. I don't know exactly at what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who, if anyone, replaced you on the bridge at Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I was replaced by Boro Nikolic, the chief's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you have a reason why it was Boro Nikolic who replaced you on the Karakaj bridge?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He just got there. Otherwise, he and the other three military policemen were at the bridge to receive and see off UNPROFOR convoys with aid that were entering Bosnia from Serbia. There were four of them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters apologise, we did not catch all the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case they were at the bridge, and they would receive UNPROFOR shipments and check them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, the interpreters says they did not understand the names that you mentioned. Can you say those names over again?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Boro Nikolic, Milenko Marjanovic, Krsto Josic, and Dragoje Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When you returned at Standard that morning, can you describe what you saw? What was the situation like?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: There was nothing special about it. It was quiet, there were no soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were there many vehicles going in and out of Standard barracks on that day?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No. The traffic was regular just like any other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you say that there were no soldiers, who was left from the brigade on that day in Standard?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: There were the mechanics of the logistics, those from the kitchen and the mess, the financial department, and a couple of administrators. It was myself and Nebojsa Jeremic who was another military policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Milic Duric?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: He was, I think -- I think he was a boss, a supervisor of the mechanics who were there working at Standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing him on that day?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you see Drago Nikolic on that day?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing Bircakovic a driver of Drago Nikolic on that day?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember having seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you see any officers who were not from the brigade but would have been from the VRS arrive at Standard on that day?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you see any civilian visitors at Standard on that day?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If a civilian had arrived in a civilian car and dressed in civilian clothes, would you have seen that civilian?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would the person on duty at the gate, would that person have seen the civilian?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What did you do at Standard that day?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Nothing much. I was in the office going about my regular tasks. I was there doing nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you know how long Jeremic was on duty at the gate in that period?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: He was there for 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What was a normal duration of the shift for the military policemen on duty at the gate?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: A regular shift would be 12 hours, and there would be two policemen in each shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you know, why did Jeremic was on duty at the gate for 24 hours then?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Because there was no one else there. He had to be there by himself for 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you know at the time who Vojislav Jekic was?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I had heard of him, but I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you have recognised him at that time?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know that person. I have never seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you know at that period, and we are talking always mid-July 1995, did you know who Ratko Vidovic was?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I had heard about him as well, but I didn't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you have recognised Ratko Vidovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, I could not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If Ratko Vidovic visited Standard dressed in civilians, would the military policemen on duty at the gate control his identity, as you explained earlier?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would have. That was the procedure that would be applied to Ratko Vidovic and anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, Mr. President, I think we can stop for the break. After the break I have about 15 minutes no more and then I can turn it over for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. We'll have a 25 minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, when we left off before the break, I asked you a question which was the following: "If Ratko Vidovic visited Standard dressed in civilians, would the military policeman on duty at the gate control his identity as you explained earlier?" Your answer was: "Yes, they would have. That was the procedure that would be applied to Ratko Vidovic and anyone else."

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would just like to get some clarification from you as to why is it, to your knowledge, that the military policemen at the gate could not miss a civilian such as Ratko Vidovic or Vojislav Jerkic coming into the Standard barracks on that day?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The military policemen treated all civilians the same, whether they were called Ratko Vidovic or anything else. The procedure was the same for all. They would identify them, ask for an ID, ask them where they wanted to go and that's it. There was no other procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. And the military policeman at the gate, did they have an opportunity to look into the cars that were coming in, or the vehicles that were coming in?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Do you mean civilian or military vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Any vehicles? Did they have an opportunity to look inside the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: There were no civilian vehicles entering the barracks. Military vehicles did, however. There were military trucks operating for the military driven by conscripts, but we were not checking those. They were on their regular duties and we knew most of them, most the drivers. We knew they were driving for the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one final question on this issue, the barrier that was lifted up or down to let vehicles in, do you know what use was made of it in July 1995? Was it ever left standing or was it always down, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The barrier was always down. Whoever approached the gate would first be seen by the military policeman on duty. If the vehicle concerned is a military one, or if it was the commander, the barrier would be lifted and as soon as the vehicle was in, it would be put down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you know who replaced Jeremic as the military policeman on duty at the gate that night? I'm talking now the day that you saw the buses.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Who replaced Jeremic or who it was that Jeremic replaced; I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise, my question was not clear. The day that you saw the buses, you mentioned before that Jeremic was on duty for, I think you said, 24 hours. Do you know when he left his duty at the gate.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Probably the next day. I don't remember at all. He was probably replaced by one of the military policemen who came back from the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that exactly leads into my next question, do you know when the members of the Military Police Company who left for Orahovac, do you know when they came back?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall the next morning, I'm talking now the day after you saw the buses, do you remember if there was a lineup on that day, as you describe earlier?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember if there was a lineup. In the course of those few days, there were no lineups because there were no people present. Everyone was in the field. In extraordinary circumstances there are no lineups.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on that morning, again the day following the day you saw the buses, were there many people at the barracks the next morning?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: There were soldiers. I saw some. There weren't all that many, I don't know how many exactly though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall when Commander Pandurevic returned from -- to the Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall on that day seeing soldiers who were not from Zvornik Brigade in Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: There were soldiers that I didn't know. I don't know where they were from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall whether you saw Drago Nikolic the next morning at Standard?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't recall really.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, in the past two years, did you have the opportunity to meet with investigators from the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 18th of January 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you sign a statement then?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall if your meeting with the investigators of the Prosecution was recorded?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: They told me that it was being recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall if you were a suspect at that time?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: They told me that I was not a suspect, but that I was there as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall the questions or what they wanted to know from you exactly?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: They were asking me questions as from the beginning of the war, where I was, what I did and up to the moment when I arrived in the Military Police Company and onwards. We spent most of the time talking about June 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: July 1995 and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you see a copy of your interview with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to read it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you remember who provided you with a copy of that interview?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you still agree today with the answers you gave to the Prosecution when you met with them?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's it more or less. There were minor mistakes, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall if the investigators asked you any questions about a duty roster?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: They did ask about that, in particular about July 1994 [sic] they wanted to know about the roster of the military police. They were particularly interested in whether any dates were deleted or erased.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just to bring a correction to the transcript, at line 15 where is says July 1994, did you say July 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I meant to say 1995. I may have said '94.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like now to show you a document which is the duty roster that was discussed during your interview with the Prosecution. Do you recall if you saw the duty roster at that time?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, for e-court I'd like to have P354, however, there is an original of this document which the Prosecution brought to the courtroom today; and I think it would be better if we gave the original to the witness and he can use the ELMO beside him to answer the next few questions, with the consent of the Prosecution, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to take a look at this document, and take a few minutes to glance at the various pages, and then I will ask you a few questions. Take the time to look at it, and then I will ask you questions.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: You can ask the question right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, who completed this attendance roster for July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you complete a roster like this for every month?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not in the initial period while I was with the military police. I don't remember when exactly I started filling these in, maybe it lasted for a year or two. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the writings on this document, are they in ink or what exactly are they -- were they written with?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I used a pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is there any specific reason why you used a pencil to fill in this document?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you explain why you used a pencil?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I used a pencil so that when the daily order is read out in the morning, there can occur certain changes to it. In this way, I make sure that if there is a change, an attack, an emergency, the entry can be erased with a rubber and a new one made. For instance, a man would go to the "cepa" called the Karakaj bridge where he would be assigned, but in the meantime there would occur an emergency and the man would have to go elsewhere, in that event I would erase what was formerly written and then make the new entry. That was the sole reason why I used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we took a look at the duty roster for the other months, are they also filled in with a pencil?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote the first and last names in ballpoint pen and the entered the dates in pencil so that they could be erased. I would normally make the roster on the evening before the relevant day, and if in the course of that day changes occurred, I could easily make the relevant corrections in pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, who -- what was the purpose of having this attendance roster? Why did you make one out?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Nobody told me to do that. I did it because I thought that I would have clear records kept in this way. I maintained the records of the company members just that I once did when I was working in an office doing my regular job. I knew that emergencies occurred where commanders would need to assign a number of military policemen to resolve a certain situation. I knew that I was able to make corrections this way. So this was my initiative to do it this way in order to avoid having incorrect entries where a man would be set to be in one place whereas he actually had to be elsewhere. That's why I made the roster. I normally made it on the evening before the eleventh day and then on the day I would report to Commander Jasikovac before the lineup. He would sign the daily order and then it would be implemented. Where such a need arose, an entry would be erased and rewritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, when you made the changes, where did you get the information that would lead you to make these changes?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: If the person was assigned to go out into the field, then I would write as much. If I knew the specific location the person was assigned to, I would make an entry of it. Let me give you an illustration. In that period of time when I knew that my brother went to the Baljkovica region with his men, I wouldn't write Baljkovica; I would merely write down out in the field since he was no longer in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, maybe my question was not precise. How did you learn the information in order to make changes? Did anyone tell you or did you find out by yourself?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Nobody would tell me anything. If somebody said that they were going out into the field, I would make an entry in the field. Nobody told me to do that, I did it for my sake alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, did you know whether the other companies or battalions in Zvornik Brigade used a similar form?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, no. This individual Misko, I believe his last name was Vasic, I went to see him; and I consulted with him about this idea of mine about keeping a rostrum, a roster. So I proceeded to use that format. I don't know if he used that similar format or not. I know that I used it for the purposes of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, when you made changes to this form, or rather allow me to be more direct, did you ever make changes to these forms with the intention of hiding information?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not concealing anything here. I wrote everything as it happened with a clear conscience. There's nothing or no one for me to hide there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall when you met with the Prosecution investigators if they asked you any specific questions about changes made to this form, the one that you have in your hands?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what questions were those?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: They asked me about Orahovac and Rocevic, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall what they wanted to know and what your answers were?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I remember vaguely. They wanted to hear from me that I had been concealing or hiding matters, which isn't what I did. I told them that nobody had instructed me to keep the information the way I did, that it was my idea and I did not have reason to hide anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall if they drew your attention on this form to the columns for the 13th -- sorry, the 14th and 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the specific questions they asked you at that time concerning these two days?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: They asked me questions about Orahovac, which is something that I corrected, and about Rocevic with Jasikovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall any questions about the use of the letter "R" which would have been erased from these records?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: They told me they sent it for forensic examination and that they uncovered a letter R beneath. This is something I don't remember. I said at the time, and I do state today, that I have no idea about the military police going down into Rocevic. I have no idea where Jasikovac was. They said that he was down at Rocevic. I guess you should ask him that. I don't know. Jasikovac was the commander of the MP Company in other words he was my commander as well, he wouldn't report to me upon his return from the field that he went to such and such a place. How should I know, the commander never informs his soldiers about his whereabouts, and things are done the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did you hear about any execution of prisoners taking place in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. I was told that it was on the following day. I forgot, it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall exactly what you heard about the topic of executions?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Not exactly. I heard that Muslims had been liquidated at Orahovac, I heard that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: According to the rumours that you heard, who did those killings?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Nobody said anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you hear any rumours about other places where executions might have taken place?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Not right away. Later on, I don't know how much later though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you give us a time estimate as to when or how long after? Is it weeks or months or more that you heard about executions in other areas?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I couldn't pinpoint the exact time. I did hear about it, but I can't tell you when, it was a long time ago, and let me tell you, I didn't much like talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, today, do you know if executions really took place in the Zvornik area back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And just to come back, just to clarify, the first time you heard about executions that might have taken place in areas other than Orahovac, how did you come about to hear these rumours?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't remember exactly. I heard of there having been executions, but I don't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, how many times did you meet with members of the Defence team of Drago Nikolic during the last two years?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Three to four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall meeting with me?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall how many times we met?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Two to three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall meeting with Mrs. Jelena Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How many times, if you know?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Likewise, three to four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you meet with the investigators of the Defence team of Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I met with them in Zvornik I think it was Keselj and another lady, I don't know her name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And all these meetings, do you put them together at three or four times or were there more than three or four times?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, I spoke with Jelena three to four times and I spoke with you two to three times, I'm not sure what you are getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe I'll be more precise. When you met with me, for example, were there other people, other members of the Defence team there present with me?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
