utterances.text: Did anyone from the Defence team of Drago Nikolic ask you to sign a statement?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: A statement? No, I didn't sign any statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what kind of questions, if you recall, were the members of the Defence team of Drago Nikolic wanted to ask you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Similar to the Prosecution, they wanted to know about the July of 1995 and the reception area at the gate, and about the work of the military police force in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you asked any questions about the roster by members of the Defence team of Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They asked me about the roster as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did members of the Defence team of Drago Nikolic tell you about anyone who had testified in this case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President I think we need to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please for His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move into private session before or after you make your intervention, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are going to need a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are in private session in any case. Already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did any members of the Defence team of Drago Nikolic try to influence your testimony in any way?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I can have just one quick minute, Mr. President, to check my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions, Mr. President. That will be it for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I may just have a moment to get the lectern.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good morning to you and, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: For the record I'll introduce myself although we met in January of 2006. My name is Nelson Thayer. I'll be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution today. The first thing I'd like to do is show you a document and that is 65 ter 3742. While we are waiting for the English to come up, sir, there we go, you'll see that this is a phone directory for the Zvornik Brigade. Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could just quickly go to the, I think it's going to be the third page of the B/C/S, there should be a blank page at the next page of the B/C/S, it's the page following that. Oh, no, okay, that's good. Thank you. Page 2 of the English, please. Do you see that document, sir, the second page?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see the listing for the military police?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we have your komandir's name, Mr. Jasikovac, your name, and the name of Nada Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to the right we see an exchange or an extension 116; what was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's the local extension. We didn't have a direct telephone number, we could be reached at the extension through the local switchboard in the Standard barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I see that these three names are all listed to the left of that 116, does that mean that any of the three of you could be reached at that particular number, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just briefly would it be the same for the rest of these listings where we have, for example, right below the military police we have the listing for the lawyers, the legal service, both of them could be reached at extension 117; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, we are done with that document. Now, just previously, sir, you told us in 2006 in the interview, and I'll just quote from page 90 of that, you said: "When I moved to the military police, my brother" and you mentioned him, Aco Kostic, your younger brother. You said: "My brother was in the military police, and simply through him I managed not to go to the frontline." Sir, it's fair to say you wanted to get into the Military Police Company because you understandably preferred being there than to being in an infantry soldier manning a trench somewhere, is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it was only natural that your brother helped you out when he could in that respect, is that also fair to say, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's move to this roster that we recently spoke about, or that you recently testified about. That's 65 ter 354. And if we could go to the next page, please. And the next page. Now, sir, you maintained this roster as part of your duties as the Military Police Company administrative clerk; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it hardly needs mentioning, sir, but there are various reasons why a unit such as yours needed to maintain such records, both for internal purposes like you said, so that there would be a listing of everybody's whereabouts, but wasn't it also necessary for the brigade to know, for example, the financial services and reinforcement and personnel organs to have an accurate accounting of your company strength and capacities?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I kept these records, but they were not handed over to supplement the personnel records. Those other records, the personnel records were the ones used for monetary purposes or let's say for the payroll. My roster had nothing to do with those payroll and other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's look at some of the symbols and abbreviation that you used in this document, and with madam usher's assistance, I'm going to give you the original again. Where we see a plus sign, sir, and if you could just go to the first page of the actual personnel listing that has your komandir, Jasikovac's name, if you have that in front of you in the original, that's what is on the screen. The plus sign or a small cross, that mean that is that individual was present in command at Standard; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where we see SL, that is short for "slobodan" or free, the person had leave?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where we see an actual T as opposed to a plus sign or a cross, that means "teren" or in the field or terrain?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, there are some other abbreviations that you used, namely "TS," and that stood for terrain Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And "TZ" stood for terrain Zepa, is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that you told us that where we see entries, for example, several TS's in a row, followed by a TZ, that meant that those MPs were providing security to the command in Zepa after they left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page, I believe it's 7 of the original. And, sir, I think in your version that's also going to be the seventh page. I wanted to go one more, please. Actually, if we could back up. There we go. Do you see the page that at the top line is number 70, looks like Zoran Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go down a little ways, we don't need to scroll, we can just look at it, we see one example of the TSs at line 81, Dragan Stevic. And a couple of more examples at lines 83 and 84, do you see those, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's what you just told us about, is that correct, those examples of providing --

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not sure if you speak English, but we need to leave a pause between my questions and your answers. This is usually a problem we have when people are speaking the same language although we are not, but you just need to wait until the translators have a chance to catch up, okay? I see my friend standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just like my colleague to confirm whether he does or does not speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it may become useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you speak any English?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So we are just being psychic. Okay. Now, if we look at line 85 -- or I'm sorry, I want to look at another abbreviation. If we look at line 82. There's a row of Ps. What does that stand for? What do the P stand for?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: It was Commander Pandurevic's cousin who was in his escort. I don't know whether he was with Pandurevic in Srebrenica and Zepa, but I used a P for the word "pratnja," which is escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. There's also an abbreviation TN, and that stands for terrain, Nisici; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That means terrain, Nisici, in the field, Nisici; two military policemen, Jovanovic and Janisic went to Nisici every fortnight there would be a rotation from Zvornik and in each shift one of them would be there, they would be free for a fortnight and then they would spend the next two weeks there, and they were kept on our files of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where is that, or what is in Nisici?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Around Sarajevo, I think, I have never been there. Our soldiers were in charge of a part of the lines there. I think they went there as security officers. I was never there, therefore I can't tell you precisely where Nisici is. They were not in the responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, I think it falls within the AOR of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just two more abbreviations to help us out with, sir, we see a B/BO, what does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: BO, sick leave. Bolovanje, the letter B in front is for "bolnica," hospital. Those were wounded and hospitalized, meaning that they were in the hospital that day for a number of days, perhaps. The rest is sick leave while at home after having been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we can see that up at line 79, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, 79, Dragan Asceric, he was on sick leave for five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we see an NO abbreviation, what does that tell us if we are looking at that roster?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That means absent without leave. An O mean that that person was not present in the unit and had not obtained the proper leave. This stands for only one person, Miodrag.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter did not catch the last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was the last name Miodrag who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just for the record he is at line 35 on a previous page, but we'll just move on. Just one last question, sir, if you go to page 3 of the document, if we could go back to ERN 6610. If you could just translate for us, if you look at line 6, Nebojsa Jeremic's line, if you go all the way to the right, can you tell us what "Radna Obaveza "is?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of July 1995, Nebojsa Jeremic was dismissed from the unit and went to attend to his tasks pertaining to work obligation. He was no longer a member of the MP unit as of the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just so we are clear on the record when you use the word "dismissed" that's not a pejorative term that's simply means he is released from the MP company so he can satisfy his work obligations; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was no longer with the army, he was a civilian who had work duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We are done with this document for now, sir. If you could just put it back in its sleeve and we'll put it to the side. Thank you. Sir, you testified in your evidence in chief that it was Komandir Jasikovac who ordered that all the MPs who were still in the barracks were to go to Orahovac and provide security for the Muslim prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Jasikovac left Standard with the MPs for Orahovac in some kind of vehicle, right, whether you can remember what it was or not, they drove there? Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in your experience, sir, from whom would Jasikovac have received that order to take his men to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell me who had issued him with that order. He just told me that we should be ready to take our weapons and to go to provide security for some POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I understand that, sir, but my question was, in your experience from whom would Jasikovac have received that order to take his men to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, you testified in your evidence in chief about the process by which the daily taskings would flow from the brigade commander's daily briefing to the security chief Drago Nikolic, and then to your Komandir Jasikovac and then down to the Military Police Company. In your experience, was there anyone else in that chain or was in your experience those individuals that you talked about the people that were responsible for the ultimate tasks and orders that the members of the Military Police Company received?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: As I said, Drago Nikolic issued him orders in peacetime when there were no -- rather when there were no extraordinary events and he would pass those down after the briefing. As for Jasikovac and who issued him orders, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, I understood your testimony in your evidence in chief to be pertaining to the 1995, in particular, the events of July 1995. So we are not talking about peacetime, sir, we are talking about July of 1995. The tasks that the Military Police Company received, in your experience, would come from Drago Nikolic to Lieutenant Jasikovac; correct.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I was talking about quiet times when there were no activities such as those on the 14th and the 15th of July. The commander was not at Standard. During quiet periods, Jasikovac received his orders from Drago. As for this period, I don't know who was ordering what to whom. I just know he told us to get ready to go and secure POWs. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did Drago Nikolic have anyone that was assisting him in his role as the security chief of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think Milorad Trbic shared his office with him. I don't know whether there was anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, during what you described as these quiet days at the brigade following the fall of the Srebrenica enclave, sir, was Milorad Trbic around?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I didn't see him. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about two of the lawyers, Goran Bogdanovic and Cedo Jovic in your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Cedo Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, forgive me for my pronunciation. When they returned from Orahovac, one of them told you that they no longer had their rifles. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I do. I remember that they reported to me, that they no longer had had rifles with them. I don't know whether they had lost them or someone had taken them from them. What I do know is that they came back without rifles, the rifles having been left in Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in your interview with the OTP, you were asked the following question, and this is at page 75: "Question: Did you speak with Cedo and Bogdanovic what was going on in Orahovac? And your answer was: "They don't like to speak about it." And you were asked: "Did you hear what happened in Orahovac?" And your answer was: "Everybody knows, everybody knows that they executed these people there. That's not an issue." You were asked: "When did you find out people were executed there? You said, "When?" The investigator said, "Yeah." You said, "After the execution. After that." You were asked, "How long after that?" And you said, "I don't know, probably the same evening that was then said, but I don't know who said it." And then later on, you said: "These people who were there probably Goran and Cedo told me. They were telling about it but they were not there but they heard what was happening." Do you stand by those answers that you gave in 2006 to us, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. I don't know, I didn't hear, I don't know whether they told me that or someone else. It was a long time ago. I don't know whether if they told me that upon their return when they reported their missing rifles. I don't remember what they were discussing, but more or less this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at the time that Lieutenant Jasikovac ordered the MPs to go to Orahovac, what was your understanding was going to happen to the people being guarded there?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: We didn't have -- he told us that we were there to secure the POWs, that was the understanding, and that's when the MPs went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My question, sir, was what was your understanding of what was going to happen to the prisoners that were being guarded in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: How could I have understood that? I don't know. Securing them, what they were going to do with them, I don't know. How could I understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, to your knowledge did any of your fellow MPs at the time tell you what they understood the -- what was going to happen with respect to those Muslim prisoners in Orahovac, even if you didn't have an understanding yourself, did you hear from any of the MPs before they went out what their understanding was of what was going to happen with those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No one was talking about it. The military policemen got ready and went in the field to Orahovac. Nobody talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, let me just share with you some of the questions and answers from your interview back in 2006. I'm going to read to you some of those questions and answers and then just put a question to you, okay? So just bear with me while I read some of this. You told us that people started to prepare to go to Orahovac and nobody was willing to go. This is at pages 64 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Page 65. And the question was put to you: "How do you know people weren't willing to go?" And your answer was: "One could see, one could see on their faces and for me it was an extremely great pleasure to hear that I should not go." And you were also asked the following question: "Question: Why didn't you go to Orahovac?" And your answer was: "I don't know, I don't know, it was my fortune." "Question: But who decided that you should stay in the brigade?" And your answer was: "The commander told me to stay. I couldn't decide. I was depending on the orders, but if he told me that I should go, with hard feeling in my heart, I would have to go. Let me tell you one more time, people knew me, and if they asked me to assist them in some way and I could not help them, of course I would feel bad. So at least I don't have a guilt conscience because of that -- guilty conscience because of that. And that's why I sleep peacefully today because I didn't take part in anything, and I didn't even see deaths, which is important to me." Now, you told us earlier about seeing the buses with the men and their heads bowed. And you also made a point of volunteering to us the following information in your interview: I quote, and this is at page 46: "Before the war I played football in the Drina and people -- people knew me from Zvornik; and I didn't want to get close to them because they might have asked me to help them, so I knew that I could not help them much, so I tried to be away." And the question was put to you: "You were speaking about the people from the bus, the Muslim people from the buses?" And your answer was: "I did not want them to ask me anything because I knew that I could not help them." Sir, you've indicated to us that you don't know what the plan was for these prisoners. Why are you talking about being so happy about not being sent there, about not seeing deaths, about not having a guilty conscience and being so powerless to help them that you wanted to avoid contact with them?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, no one knew of the liquidations. When we were told to go to provide security, nobody was talking about it and it had nothing to do with the liquidations. I'm speaking of myself when I say that I was glad not to go. One doesn't feel comfortable if you are, for example, recognised and then they say Stevo help us, and at that point I could not help them at all. That's why I said that. I see nothing bad about having said that. I'm glad for not being up there. I didn't know what was going to take place, nobody did, we were there to provide security. There were people there, they could have asked for help and I was nothing but a private. We were only providing security nothing more. Nothing that I have to add to that. And I can tell you this, people went knowing that they were going up there to provide security. It's something that may require spending your whole night there, that's why people were not happy to go. Nobody was talking about any killings, only about providing security. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During this period of time did you ever hear that these prisoners were going to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No one was talking about anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During this period of time, sir, that you described as being a quiet one in the brigade, you know that there was this column of thousands and thousands of Muslim men and boys that was breaking through to free territory right in the rear of the Zvornik Brigade, passing just to the west of Zvornik itself; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's why the barracks were so deserted during this period of time; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And soldiers were being sent everywhere from Snagovo and Miricici all the way up to Baljkovica, right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: To Baljkovica, yes, that is correct. I don't know exactly where they were, but they were in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And they were in the brigade trying to send basically every last person they could afford to send into the field; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I know that the military police force went out into the field. I don't know about others, where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I mean, that's why they had to send lawyers to guard prisoners and a lawyer to stand at the gate; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's true as far as the military policemen are concerned because the entire force was engaged in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was there anything that you are aware of that would have prevented you from being sent to Snagovo or Baljkovica? Or any other place that was facing active combat?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: How should I know? I stayed behind at Standard. When a lawyer was asking me about it, I said that I went into the field myself as the need arose. When the frontline was attacked. At that time, though, I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you described how relieved you were that you didn't have to go to Orahovac, that's a fair description; right? You were actually more than relieved that you didn't have to go to Orahovac for the reasons that I read out to you that you told us in your interview, right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that I was glad not to have gone there. Why? Well, because people there may have known me, been my acquaintances or perhaps not. That was the reason why I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, you told us in your interview that during this period of time you were basically trying to stay out of sight at Standard because the more somebody might see you, the greater the chance was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Reference please, from the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can provide that in a moment, but if I can move on. I can tell you it's in the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon is not very happy with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just like if he is going to put a question, say something to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it arose actually during the course of the colloquy with the witness so--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are wasting more time discussing this. If you could look up the reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Then, if you give me a moment, Mr. President, I'll consult --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tell you something about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said that, namely that I didn't like much to mill about the Standard compound, I didn't mean to say that I was hiding. I couldn't have been hiding. I was mobilised, I was there. You said that I was hiding. I may have stated something similar, but this isn't what I meant. I was in the Standard barracks and I didn't have reason to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, given the answer, may I move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, would you have rather gone to guard prisoners at Orahovac or gone to Baljkovica at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I wouldn't have liked to have gone anyway because in Baljkovica you could see for yourself the list how many wounded and how many were killed, including my brother, Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That is exactly right, sir, those Muslims had guns that were firing in Baljkovica, those in Orahovac did not; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for the record, Mr. President, the cite is page 79 of the interview, line 11: "The best was not to go out much because I was not on the frontline, and if I go much out somebody can notice that and sent me so it was the best to be in the office, in a way hide." That's from lines 8 to 12. Do you remember saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Something along those lines. I'm not sure if that's exactly it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's return to the attendance roster. If we could have 65 ter 354, please. You told us during your interview that and I quote at page 83: "I was writing the names who was free, or who was available. That's what I was doing. That is what I was doing according to the order of the commander of the company." And later again at page 88, you told us: "I was entering things that was in accordance with Jasikovac entering, and nobody else was ordering me anything. Only Jasikovac." Do you recall those answers, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: As far as the lists go, I wrote them. I said that, and let me repeat, it is so happened that in the course of the day an emergency would arise, somebody had to go somewhere, and the list had to make a correct entry of how many policemen were in the barracks and how many were outside. This was something that I could not know or ascertain right away from the records that were otherwise kept. That's why I had my own records. I may have shown them to Jasikovac as well, it was a long time ago. I don't recall how exactly these things worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, you testified in your evidence in chief about the daily lineup and the reading out of the daily tasks. I think you told us, and this has been confirmed by other MPs, that you would be the one who would be reading out where individual MPs would be tasked or where they would be located on a given day, and that was in the morning; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where did you receive the information that you would be entering on to this roster and then reading out during the morning muster?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I drafted the roster in the office every evening for the following day. The roster stated who should be doing what and where. I had the approval of the commander of the Military Police Company to do that, he would have a look at it, sign it, and then I would read it out in the morning. When I was drafting them in the evening, I would enter the various tasks on the expected dates in pencil so that I could readily change whatever needed to be possibly changed. I would get a signature from the commander and would then proceed to read out what was on the list. There was no other method of work than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Simple question, sir. That information that you would enter about where people were tasked came from Jasikovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I wrote that. He only checked what I wrote and said if he agreed or not. I was the one who kept track of the whereabouts of the members of the MP company, and I made sure that they rotated doing the various tasks so that not always the same person would be doing the same thing. He was the one who signed these daily orders, and then I read them out in the morning. I was producing those on my own. Nobody was telling me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Right. But, sir, your testimony is not that you were the one who is making up the assignments, sending people to terrain Zepa or terrain Srebrenica or Orahovac; right? You are not the one who is originating those orders?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's right. What I'm telling you, though, is that I was doing that too in peacetime whenever there were no combat activities and when there were no daily orders to be given, it was only in those moments of quiet that such daily orders would be made. Whenever somebody had to go out into the field of the MP company, then I would bring a list to Jasikovac, and he would be the one picking and choosing those who would have to go and do that particular task in the field. But as for the daily orders, I was the one drafting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, we will again look at that roster and I'll ask you some specific questions about who gave you orders about certain destinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we are coming up to the break I'm being told that we may have a couple of minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have the break now and we'll continue later. 25 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You told us in your interview that the log that we've been talking about was the official duty roster or attendance log for the company; there was nothing else, that was it what we've been looking at and talking about, and that's at page 84. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The attendance in the unit, yes. As for the other documents, for the unit they were kept by the military policemen, that was the so-called VOB 8 list. In other words, this wasn't the only list kept by the military police force, there were others.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when you refer to the VOB 8 list, what are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: It's a large book containing all the information. The person's name, father's name, date of mobilisation, date of entry on duty in the military police force. This was kept by the personnel service. I don't know what else I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Right. But can you confirm what you told us in 2006, sir, that the log we have been talking about that you've been looking at is the only official attendance duty log for the Military Police Company?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. This was something that I kept as part of the daily order, and I had records of my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you admitted to us in your interview, sir, that you alone were responsible for the erasures on the log, erasing those entries and replacing them with different ones; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can I have a reference in the interview, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sure. Page 68, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you specifically admitted originally writing "O" for Orahovac for certain MPs on certain days and then erasing the "O" and replacing it with a "T" for terrain; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you haven't changed your story about that, as you sit here today; correct? You stand by that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did that. I wrote that. There's no problem in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you also told us in 2006 that you didn't know what the Rs referred to which were erased; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If my colleague is going to use the interview, he should quote from the interview so the witness knows exactly what are the words that he used, and it would be much better for the witness so that he knows what he said then, and then he can comment on it; thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it is much better if you adopted what Mr. Bourgon is suggesting. I mean, after all, we've had such instances before and this is the preferred way of dealing with witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll be happy to do that and if I may continue my questioning along these lines; and I will refer to that shortly, and I will put these specific questions and answers to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, it's your testimony today, is it not, that you didn't know then and you don't know now what the erased Rs referred to?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes. I still claim that today. I don't know anything about an R, anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge, sir, about Zvornik Brigade MPs being sent to Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, that would include knowledge that you may have had at the time, up and to the time you are sitting today, is it your testimony that even today you have no information whatsoever about Zvornik Brigade MP Company soldiers going to the Rocevic School?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during your interview you stressed that this roster was something that you kept for your own personal use. Today you said it was "my initiative," I think is how you referred to it. And if we are looking for cites, I can say at page 16 you said: "I was filling in this list just for myself." At page 20, "this is something I was filling out without anybody's order, I did it for myself." Same page "nobody ordered me to do so. This is something that I myself did." Page 55, "I was maintaining this list for myself just if someone asks in the future." Page 56 "I was maintaining it more for myself?" Page 57 "I myself did it. Nobody told me to do it." Now, sir, during this interview given your insistence which you've echoed today that you had just sort of done this on your own, I asked you a specific question, I said: "This form existed before you came to the company, is that correct." And your answer was, "No, that's not correct." And then I asked you, "So you are telling us that you designed this entire form?" And you told us then, and I believe that's what you told us today, and this is at page 57 that, "A man drew it on a computer for me and I just later filled it in. Nobody else in the barracks maintained it that way." And I think what you said today was, you identified a Misko possibly last name Vasic and you went to see him and you said: "I consulted with him about this idea of mine, about keeping a rostrum, a roster." And that was in answer to the question, "Did you know whether the other companies or battalions in the Zvornik Brigade used a similar form?" And your answer was, "No, I didn't know." I want to show you a couple of documents and with madam usher's assistance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, was there a question with that, or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the question is coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think it's obvious, Mr. President, the question is on its way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's coming. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: To save some time, Mr. President, and I'll make it a little easier, I'm just asking we put these on the ELMO, I don't think technically we can do what I want to do on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll put them on the ELMO. No problem with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at the top we have 65 ter 354, which we've been looking at. In the upper right-hand corner you can see this is the military police log that we've been looking at. And the second document for the record is the Zvornik Brigade engineering company attendance roster for July 1995. Do you see that, sir? This is 65 ter 2851 for the record. In the upper right-hand corner, do you see where it says "engineering company"?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: These are identical forms, are they not?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to show you 65 ter 3726. With madam usher's help. That is the logistics -- please, just replace. We see we have an identical form, do we not, being used by the logistics organ, also for July 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you the first battalion signal squad attendance roster for the month of July. That's 65 ter 3760. Same form, right, sir? We need an audible answer, it's the same form, right, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that. I don't know -- I told you that I kept these records. I had no idea of them having it as well. Perhaps Misko did it for them as well, but it doesn't really matter if they did, I can see now that they did have the same form, but what difference does it make? What has it got to do with it? When he produced this for me on the computer, I didn't know he had other forms like that. Perhaps he made others for them after he had done some for me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, sir, this form, as you can see wasn't something that you alone were just using for your own purposes. Every unit, and I can go through all eight battalions and pull out battalion logs and squad logs that all use the same form. Everybody had to use this same form because it was a critical way of accounting for the whereabouts and capacities of the units; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, I have nothing to do with their forms. I didn't know that they kept these records. I knew -- I know that I did. I don't know when they started keeping records. They used a ballpoint pen I can see, whereas I used a pencil. I really wasn't aware of the other units keeping these records. Perhaps they obtained the same forms from Misko or perhaps they took the same forms that I used. I wasn't told by anyone of them using them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it your testimony as somebody that has spent as much time as you did as the administrative clerk for the Military Police Company that you can't tell the Trial Chamber why these forms were important to all these other battalions and units maintaining these rosters?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know why they kept them. I know why I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it's your testimony that all these other units on their own just got the initiative that you say you had to get these forms made up and used them for exactly the same purposes? That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the same question was asked and answered a number of times and this is not what the witness said. If he wants to ask him this as a question, that's fine. But not to say that this is what you said today. I mean, we've been labouring this point now over and over again, I let my colleague work, but I think it's quite clear what the witness knows and doesn't know about this form.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question is a simple one and it's clear I think the witness is capable of answering it. It's my last question on the topic and I just want to see if we can get an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For me it is an irrelevant question. I really don't know what the others kept. I know why I kept these forms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to your next question, Mr. Thayer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to remind you, sir, of some of the different answers and explanations you gave to us during your interview in 2006 when we asked you about alterations.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm going to read you some passages, it might take a few moments, but I'll have some questions for you when I'm done putting the actual questions to you. You were asked at page 53: "Question: But tell me why did you erase the letter O and put in T?" And your answer was: "Answer: Believe me, I don't remember." Follow up question was put: "Question: But Mr. Stevo, it doesn't make sense the letter O and then put the letter T. Why did you change the duty roster ?" And your answer was: "Answer: I don't know; believe me I don't know why I was doing it." That's at page 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, if my colleague is going to cite from the interview, he should read the complete questions and answers and not just part of them, now he is jumping the beginning of the question, the beginning of the answer, the beginning of the question and beginning of the answer; he should read the whole text and ask the witness to confirm one question at a time and not in a box session. Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him proceed the way he chooses and then if it's necessary to intervene, we will intervene, or else you can raise the issue on redirect. I think it's better we have to respect the fact that -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will try to explain maybe better what the issue I have with this. In this part, my colleague said he read the question: "But tell me why did you erase the letter O and put T?" Then he read the witness's answer, "Believe me I don't remember." Then he jumped to the next question omitting the fact that the witness gave an explanation, "As you see all these people were on T, terrain, but not all of them were in Orahovac that day." If he jumps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's not fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop, you can deal with this on redirect if you want, Mr. Bourgon. But otherwise please don't interfere with the way he is conducting his cross-examination unless we tell we allow you to do so. Mr. Thayer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, your answer to the question, I'll just repeat the question: "Question: Why did you changes duty roster?" Your answer was: "Answer: I don't know. Believe me, I don't know why I was doing it." That's at page 54. You were asked a follow-up question: "Question: And the same of letter R?" And you answer: "Answer: The letter R was not written definitely because I don't know what would the letter R mean." And it was put to you in the next question, "It means Rocevic." And you answered: "Answer: I guarantee you no police officers were in Rocevic on that day." Then you go on to say: "But I don't know who was there, maybe they were sent from somewhere else but from the barracks they didn't go to Rocevic." Again that's on page 54. You deny writing in the letter R and erasing it and you say: "It is possible that they were sent from Orahovac, but I don't know about it. I just know for that Orahovac." That's at page 55. Then you go on to say "For me, all the people who were not in the barracks were in the field. Why did I do it? I don't know. I don't have a reason to do it. If I wanted to do it, I would rip the paper off. I do not hide it." That was at page 55. You were asked again later, this is at page 78: "Question: Do you recall why did you alter these records?" And your answer was: "Answer: I don't know. I really did not have any intentions to hide anybody. People you were changing their assignment and that's why sometimes things were erased and things were entered." And then in another series you give the following explanations, this is at page 84 the question was put to you, sir: "Question: So you are telling us that you originally wrote O for the people you told us about before who had gone up to Orahovac?" And your answer was: "Answer: I wrote down everything. I did not think, I was just listening what my commander was saying. I wasn't commander. I was the only one who was writing everything on this page." On page 86 again you say: "If I wanted to hide somebody, I would just throw this paper away or rip it off or somehow destroy it." And then you were asked again: "Question: We'd like to ask you again why you erase the letters on this log?" And your answer: "Answer: I really don't know what to tell you. I was writing the letters, and I don't know what happened to me that I erase it and I put a new letter. All of them went to the terrain, so I don't know. I don't have a clue." And that's at page 89. You were asked: "Question: Do you remember when you made the changes?" That's at page 89 again. You were answer was: "Answer: Immediately when it happened. Immediately when it happened. If they told me it was a change or something I immediately erase things, and I put for terrain or something else." Now, sir, you've had an opportunity to look at the log. You've seen the Os that have been erased and you have seen the Rs that have been erased, right? We know that from looking at the document, tell me if you disagree. For Jasikovac on 14 July the O was changed to a T, and on the 15 July the R was changed to a T. For Nada Stojanovic, on 14 July, the O was changed to a T. Under Goran Bogdanovic, 14 July, the O was changed to a T. Cero Jovic, 14 July, the O was changed to a T. Under Dragoje Ivanovic, 14 July, the O was changed to a T. And on the 15th July, the R was changed to a T. Under Predrag Ristic, 14 July, you changed the O to a T; and on the 15th July, the R is erased and replaced with a T. Zelko Stevanovic, 14 July, the O is changed to a T. And under Milomir Simic, 14 July, O changed to a T; 15 July, R change today a T. Stanoje Bircakovic, 14 July, O changed to a T; 15 July, R changed to a T. Sladan Jokic, 14 July, O changed to a T; and 15 July, changed to a T. Now, sir when you went through this log, sir, you remembered that certain of these people actually went to Orahovac; correct.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: You've put many questions to me, I hope I'll remember all of them to answer them. The answers I've been giving to you two years ago when you've been just reading out is something I'm agree with and this is something I'll repeat now. Whenever Jasikovac said that the place to go to was to be Orahovac, I don't remember today, I only recall Bogdanovic Goran, Nada Stojanovic, Jasikovac. I remember for a fact, that they did go there; for the others I have no idea, when I look at the list of the military police that is when I realise they were up there. And let me tell you this as well, our soldiers who were out in the field and for whom I had a rough idea of where they were, I would make an entry T, terrain or out in the field, simply to make a note of the fact that they were not at the Standard barracks, that's why I wrote that. I didn't have a single reason to hide anything, and I repeat I didn't have any idea of anyone going to Rocevic. If they did go there, then they must have gone there from Orahovac. To me, they were out in the field, that's what I knew. I don't know how it is that I can assure you that this is the truth other than tell you that I swore to tell the truth and nothing but the truth and I'm telling the truth. I would have been telling you the truth even though I had not taken an oath. It is not a contested matter any more. Everybody knows now who it is who was at Orahovac, they were there and that's a one hundred percent certainty. But to hint that I am hiding anything or cover up anything, no. The fact is that the names you read out must have been there though when I think back about that time, I know about the four individuals having gone to Orahovac and for others I'm not too sure. When you gave me the list in Zvornik it was only at that point when I was able to consult the list a bit that I realized what had happened and that I told you it was only me who drafted the list. As for Rocevic, I didn't know at all that the military police force went there. You must have someone to ask that question to. I myself can tell you once more that I have no idea who went there, if anybody went there. I don't know what else I can tell you on that score. But what I am telling you is something I know and I'm sure of one hundred percent, and there's no reason why I should be covering up for anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, at the beginning of your answer, you indicated that it was Jasikovac who was telling you that certain people were going to Orahovac, and that's why you put the O in the first place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: It is possible. It is possible that I did it that way and then later I marked that they were in the field. I don't know what they were doing in Orahovac. They were going there to provide security, I don't know what they were doing, if you understand me. They told us we were going to secure POWs and that's it. Later on I changed the letters, I put Ts in for field. They were all in the field. There were not in the barracks. For me they were all the same, they were all in the field. That was probably why I did it, I had no other reason to cover up for anyone, why, when everything is known?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, at the time that this order was given to send the MPs to Orahovac, you've already told us that you are not the originator of that order certainly; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Of course. Who am I to issue any orders? I was a private [as interpreted]. I was told to go to Orahovac as well, I was told to go. I would have left with difficult feelings but I would have gone, nevertheless. Had he told me to go to the bridge, I would have. I had to. It was wartime, and it's the army. Jasikovac ordered that, not me. I never issued orders. I only saw Jasikovac's orders through. Maybe I did pass on an order to a soldier because it had come from Jasikovac, but I never issued order, who was I to order anything? We had our commander and his deputy, but his deputy was not issuing many orders. He had his commander, the company commander who was in charge of that. I only kept records of the MP company during quiet periods when they were in Standard, when there were no military operations underway and then that would be signed by the commander. In extraordinary situation that was all erased and done anew because things did not go as planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've spoken about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just a correction for the transcript, Mr. President. At page 81 line 3 the record reads, "I was a private," and I'm informed what the witness said was I am a simple soldier. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In our case it's line 5 in the transcript that I have at least it's line 5 on page 81. Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We have both Mr. President, line 5 and line 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm glad we are clear on actually who was issuing the tasks. So my question then is, who told you to write the Os for Orahovac on the log? You weren't issuing those orders, you weren't generating those orders, so who told you to write the O in the first place to indicate that MPs were to be sent and were being sent to Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: As I've said many times I was doing it all. I wasn't told to do that by anyone, I was putting those things in, and I don't remember why I erased them. I put them in, I erased them. To the effect people were in the field. I didn't order them to go to Orahovac, who was I to do that; Jasikovac did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is Jasikovac still alive, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He is alive, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to ask him all this. He will tell you everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know where Jasikovac is today?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen him since my demobilisation in 1996. I don't know where he is. He is probably still with the army. He was a professional officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you referred, sir, to the order to go to Orahovac to secure the prisoners. You told us in your interview that among your various duties as administrative clerk was dealing with arranging to pick up things from logistics or to issue a meal or weapons, ammunition, and that you also had a warehouse where you kept ammunition and weapons and that you were in charge of all of that. That's at page 7 of the interview. Sir, you are, no doubt, familiar with the role of the MPs with respect to POWs. Was any food requisitioned to bring to the prisoners? You were there at Standard during this period of time, there were a great many prisoners there, what efforts were made to bring food to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: When the military policeman went to Orahovac, they had their rifles. Each policeman had been issued with an automatic rifle and each rifle had its serial number. They had their rifles and ammunition. We didn't issue any additional ammo at that time. If needed, it was myself who went to the logistics departments to take ammunition if we needed it for the unit. The same goes for any food. I would take those and issue them to the soldiers. As for the food for the prisoners, I have no idea about that, I couldn't be issued with any food for POWs, I could only receive food for the MP members.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on your knowledge and recollection, sir, after all these discussions that you've had, there was no food requisitioned for those prisoners, was there?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I didn't see it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were asked some questions about the day you were sent to the UNPROFOR checkpoint at the bridge. And you talked about the night that the order was given to go to Orahovac and you discussed the next day and your activities at the bridge and then some activities in the brigade command. Now, my colleague didn't put any dates at all to you about this period of time, and I take it, sir, that's because you, as you sit here today, can't tell us what those dates were with any precision. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: You are right, how can I remember any exact dates 13 years ago. I can't remember the dates of a few days back let alone a few years.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it's fair to say, sir, that you can't account for all the comings and goings at the brigade command during this period of days, can you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: If I saw someone, I did. Otherwise I can't tell you I did. I was there. Had I seen anyone, I would have known about it; but I didn't see anyone, there was no one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, during this period of time after you returned from the bridge, you resumed your normal duties; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Standard going about my regular tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I don't mean to be facetious, sir, but you weren't staring out your window the entire time during those few days, were you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move to your next question, Mr. Thayer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, if you can't account for all the comings and goings at the brigade command because of you doing your own duties, then when you testified earlier today that you would have seen a civilian, had a civilian arrived in a civilian car and dressed in civilian clothes, that's not true, is it, sir? You couldn't have possibly been in a position to see at all points during that period, those days, everybody that was coming in and out of the brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Had there been a civilian in a civilian car, he would not have been let inside the barracks, for sure. I explained to you what the procedure was when a policeman appears at the gate with a civilian car. He would not be let in, inside the Standard barracks. As for whether I would have been able to see that person, I may have, but I had not seen anyone, any civilians within the perimeter during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that you told us what the procedure would have been, but my question is simple. You were in no position to see every vehicle or every visitor that came to the brigade command during that period of days, were you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know what to tell you. I could have seen someone if I had happened to be in the MP office. I could have seen someone entering the command building. But on the other hand, I may not have; I may have been doing something else, by really doubt that there was anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, isn't it possible if somebody came for a short visit, just like you said, you may not have seen that person arrive because you were busy doing other things?

utterances.speaker: STEVO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see anyone. I didn't see anyone. But as I told you, such a person would not have been let inside the barracks in a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it you have re-examination, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have to leave it until tomorrow. Tomorrow we'll reconvene at 9 o'clock in the morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. President, can the witness be warned the usually warning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Kostic, it's important that between today and -- I'll start again. It's important since we haven't finished your testimony today and you need to continue tomorrow, between now and then you do not discuss the substance of your testimony with anyone. And that means neither in person nor over the phone, neither here nor with any other witnesses that may be here present in The Hague. You are not allowed to discuss anything pertaining to this case with them. Did you understand me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
